prompt: Give a code example in Java that illustrates dependency injection with Spring.
completion:
Below is a **minimal, self‑contained Spring‑Boot example** that shows how Spring’s dependency‑injection (DI) mechanism works.  
We’ll:

1. Define an abstraction (`GreetingService`).  
2. Create a concrete implementation (`SimpleGreetingService`).  
3. Inject that implementation into a consumer (`GreeterClient`).  
4. Run the whole thing from a `SpringBootApplication`.

---

## 1. Maven `pom.xml`

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
         https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>di-demo</artifactId>
  <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>

  <parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.3.0</version>
  </parent>

  <properties>
    <java.version>17</java.version>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <!-- Spring Boot Starter (includes core, DI, etc.) -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <!-- For @ComponentScan, @Service, @Autowired, etc. -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-aop</artifactId>
      <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>
    <!-- Test support -->
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>
```

> **Tip:** Use Java 17 or newer (Spring Boot 3.x requires it).

---

## 2. Domain: Service Interface

```java
package com.example.di;

public interface GreetingService {
    String greet(String name);
}
```

---

## 3. Concrete Implementation

```java
package com.example.di;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

/**
 * Spring will automatically detect this class and register it
 * as a bean of type GreetingService.
 */
@Service   // <-- Marks the class as a candidate for DI
public class SimpleGreetingService implements GreetingService {

    @Override
    public String greet(String name) {
        return "Hello, " + name + "! Welcome to Spring DI.";
    }
}
```

> **Why `@Service`?**  
> It’s a specialization of `@Component` that semantically indicates a service‑layer bean. Spring scans for it (see `@SpringBootApplication` below) and registers it.

---

## 4. Consumer (Client) that Needs the Service

```java
package com.example.di;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

/**
 * The client will receive an instance of GreetingService
 * automatically injected by Spring.
 */
@Component
public class GreeterClient {

    private final GreetingService greetingService;

    /**
     * Constructor injection – preferred over field injection.
     *
     * @param greetingService the bean that will be injected
     */
    public GreeterClient(GreetingService greetingService) {
        this.greetingService = greetingService;
    }

    public void printGreeting(String name) {
        System.out.println(greetingService.greet(name));
    }
}
```

> **Constructor Injection**  
> - Clear and immutable dependencies.  
> - Easier to test (you can pass mocks directly).  
> - Spring automatically wires the argument because there’s only one bean of type `GreetingService`.

---

## 5. The Bootstrap Class

```java
package com.example.di;

import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

/**
 * The @SpringBootApplication annotation does a few things:
 *  - @Configuration: marks this class as a source of bean definitions.
 *  - @EnableAutoConfiguration: tells Spring Boot to auto‑configure the context.
 *  - @ComponentScan: scans the current package (and sub‑packages) for @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, etc.
 */
@SpringBootApplication
public class DiDemoApplication implements CommandLineRunner {

    private final GreeterClient greeterClient;

    public DiDemoApplication(GreeterClient greeterClient) {
        this.greeterClient = greeterClient;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DiDemoApplication.class, args);
    }

    @Override
    public void run(String... args) {
        // Use the injected client
        greeterClient.printGreeting("Alice");
    }
}
```

**What happens at runtime?**

1. `SpringApplication.run(...)` creates an `ApplicationContext`.  
2. Spring scans `com.example.di` for beans: it finds `SimpleGreetingService` and `GreeterClient`.  
3. It sees that `GreeterClient` needs a `GreetingService` and automatically injects the `SimpleGreetingService` instance.  
4. The `CommandLineRunner` (our `DiDemoApplication`) gets the `GreeterClient` bean injected into its constructor.  
5. When `run()` is called, we get the message printed.

---

## 6. Run the Application

```bash
mvn spring-boot:run
```

Output:

```
Hello, Alice! Welcome to Spring DI.
```

---

## 7. A Few Variations

| Goal | Change |
|------|--------|
| **Field injection** | Add `@Autowired` on a field inside `GreeterClient`. (Not recommended for production.) |
| **Interface‑level configuration** | Create a `@Configuration` class with a `@Bean` method that returns a `GreetingService`. |
| **Multiple implementations** | Define `@Primary` or use `@Qualifier` to tell Spring which one to inject. |
| **External configuration** | Use `@Value("${greeting.prefix:Hello}")` to inject values from `application.yml`. |

---

## Recap

- **DI** means “the container decides which implementation to supply to a dependent component.”
- **Annotations** (`@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`) make the beans discoverable.
- **Constructor injection** is the cleanest and most testable way to express dependencies.
- Spring’s **`ApplicationContext`** automatically wires everything together.

Happy coding! 🚀
